fixes.explanation: That's a fair guess, friend, but David doesn't say it here. He says, "I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations…" Then he says it again with "…among the peoples." So the praise goes out among nations and peoples.
Not this time, friend. God's first words from His sanctuary are, "I will triumph!" That's not a warning at all. It's a declaration, and it comes right at the start.
That's the word: "over Philistia I shout in triumph." It echoes how God opened, with "I will triumph!" The same word shows up at the start and again here in verse 9. Triumph, friend, from the top.

I can see why you'd pick it, since the verse is full of loud, big action. But the word the psalm gives is "triumph." God says, "over Philistia I shout in triumph." It matches how He began: "I will triumph!"

The Jordan doesn't show up in this psalm. David asks, "Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?" So the other place he names is a fortified city. I think he's asking who's got the directions, because I'd be asking the same thing.

That's his reason: "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." He's asking God for aid, and he says why in the same breath. I think that's a man who knows where to look. David says it plainly, and so does the psalm.

Chariots are a big deal in a battle, friend, but they aren't in this psalm. David asks, "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." That's the reason he gives. He says the help of man is worthless.

David doesn't say that here, friend. His words are, "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." The reason he gives is that the help of man is worthless. Mocking isn't mentioned in these verses.
